acceptable.choice: Java 21 + Spring Boot (Spring Web MVC) on the bank's standard service template, deployed to the existing OpenShift clusters
acceptable.why: It is the approved standard and the team's strongest skill, and 800 req/s with a p99 under 150 ms for a read-only lookup is routine for a single Spring Boot service with a few replicas.

acceptable.choice: Spring Boot with Java 21 virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled) and plain JDBC / Spring Data JDBC or JdbcTemplate against the Postgres replica
acceptable.why: Gives simple blocking code with good concurrency and no new technology, as long as the HikariCP pool is sized for the replica rather than for the request rate.

acceptable.choice: Read-only Spring Data JPA, if that is the house pattern
acceptable.why: Fine for a simple lookup by key, provided the queries are checked and not over-fetching; JDBC is simpler for a status read.

acceptable.choice: JVM tuning (container-aware heap settings, right-sized requests and limits, CDS/AppCDS or Spring AOT for startup) to answer the 'lighter' concern
acceptable.why: This tackles memory and startup inside the approved stack, without a new language.

acceptable.choice: Spring WebFlux + R2DBC, but only if a team already uses it
acceptable.why: It is still Java and Spring and it works, but at this load it adds reactive complexity for no real gain, so it should not be the default.

acceptable.choice: A short-TTL in-process cache (e.g. Caffeine) for non-final statuses, added only if measurement shows the replica needs it
acceptable.why: It is a cheap, approved-stack way to protect the replica, but it has to match the business rules on how fresh a payment status must be.

ruled_out.why: It is not on the approved-technology list and would need a months-long security review. It also adds a second toolchain, a second set of libraries and CVE scans, and a second skills pool to a 600-engineer Java organisation. 'Lighter' brings no benefit the requirement needs, since the JVM easily meets 800 req/s and p99 < 150 ms.

ruled_out.choice: Rust, Node.js/TypeScript, Python or any other non-approved language
ruled_out.why: Same problem: it breaks the approved-list and security-review constraint and fragments skills, with no requirement that calls for it.

ruled_out.choice: Kotlin or Scala, unless already approved
ruled_out.why: They run on the JVM but are still new languages that the architecture board must review; there is no benefit to justify that here.

ruled_out.choice: Quarkus, Micronaut or Helidon in place of Spring Boot, unless on the approved list
ruled_out.why: They break the Spring Boot standard and need board approval, and the lower footprint they offer is not needed at this scale.

ruled_out.choice: GraalVM native image as a requirement
ruled_out.why: It is not needed to meet the SLO, may itself need approval, and makes building, debugging and reflection-heavy libraries harder. Use it only if it is approved and there is a proven memory or startup need.

ruled_out.choice: Public-cloud serverless or managed services (Lambda, Cloud Run, etc.)
ruled_out.why: The bank runs on on-premises OpenShift in two data centres, and banking data residency and compliance rules apply.

ruled_out.choice: Introducing a new datastore or CQRS read model (Redis, Elasticsearch, Kafka-fed materialized view) up front
ruled_out.why: It adds unapproved or extra infrastructure and new consistency risks before anyone has shown that the existing Postgres replica can't meet the SLO.

must_mention: Recommend Java 21 + Spring Boot: it is the standard, it is approved, and the organisation's skills, tooling, security scanning, observability and on-call practice already support it.
800 req/s with p99 < 150 ms is a modest load for a read-only lookup. The JVM and Spring Boot meet it comfortably with a few pods, so language speed is not the deciding factor.

The real latency and capacity risks are in the database path: indexed queries on the replica, connection-pool sizing against the replica's max connections, network hops, and replication lag. Language choice does not fix any of these.

Go is not on the approved list. Choosing it means a months-long security review plus a long-term cost in a second toolchain, dependency and CVE pipeline, and talent pool, all for a 'lighter' benefit the requirement doesn't need.

Address 'lighter' directly: memory per pod and startup time are small costs on existing OpenShift capacity, and they can be tuned inside the JVM (heap sizing, CDS/AOT, virtual threads) if they matter.
Replica staleness has to be handled explicitly. The business must define how stale a payment status may be, because the mobile app may otherwise show an out-of-date status after a payment.

Plan for two data centres: deploy to both, with each data centre reading a local replica if one exists, and define behaviour when a replica fails or lags (timeouts, circuit breaker, fallback or clear error).

Banking requirements: authentication and authorisation so customers can only see their own payments (OAuth2/JWT via the existing gateway), audit logging, PII and data-masking in logs, rate limiting, and the bank's standard observability (metrics, tracing, latency SLO dashboards).
Prove the SLO with a load test against a production-like replica at peak and above (e.g. 2–3x 800 req/s), measuring p99 end to end, rather than arguing from benchmarks.
red_flags: Recommending Go (or another unapproved language) because it is 'faster' or 'lighter' without weighing the approval process, security review, support model and skills cost.
Claiming or implying that Java or Spring Boot cannot reliably handle 800 req/s at p99 < 150 ms.
Suggesting the team build the service in Go first and seek approval later, or otherwise get around the architecture board or security review.
Citing generic language micro-benchmarks as evidence, while ignoring that latency will be dominated by the database and the network.
Pushing reactive programming, native image, or a new framework as necessary for performance when the load doesn't require it.
Adding new infrastructure (Redis, a new database, a service mesh feature) without measurement or approval.
Ignoring replication lag and data freshness for payment status, a customer-facing and complaint-sensitive piece of financial data.
Leaving out security and compliance basics: customer-level authorisation, audit trails, PII handling in logs.
Recommending public-cloud or managed services that conflict with on-premises deployment.
Presenting a polyglot 'right tool for each job' policy as obviously good for a regulated 600-engineer organisation with a governed technology list.
unknowns: Whether the queries the endpoint needs are indexed on the replica, and their actual latency under concurrent load.
How much extra read load and how many connections the existing Postgres replica can take without hurting its current consumers.
Typical and worst-case replication lag, and how stale a status the business and mobile UX can accept.
Whether there is a replica in each data centre, and whether the service should run active-active or active-passive.
The burst profile behind the 800 req/s peak (e.g. app-open storms, push-notification spikes) and how much headroom is needed.
Whether Go, Quarkus, GraalVM native image, virtual threads or caches like Caffeine are already on the approved list.
The authentication and authorisation flow from the mobile app (gateway, token validation, entitlement checks) and its latency budget within the 150 ms p99.
Whether the 150 ms p99 is measured at the service or end to end through the gateway and the mobile network.
Per-pod resource quotas or cost pressure on OpenShift that would make the JVM's memory footprint a real concern.
